entries.seminar_title: Export Bans for Industrial Development: Evidence from Indonesian Nickel
entries.speaker: Patrick Farrell
entries.abstract: I study the consequences of Indonesia's nickel ore export ban. Manufacturing increased sharply following the ban, largely attributable to the entry of smelters. However, villages near new smelters saw declining public-goods provision, worsening infrastructure, and rising pollution, consistent with strain on local governments. While manufacturing output grew, this growth was entirely attributable to processed nickel products as other manufacturing output fell. I use export transaction records and firm ore purchase declarations to estimate a model of two-sided market power to decompose smelter margins into output markups and input markdowns. The ban's mixed record offers lessons for countries considering similar policies.

entries.seminar_title: The eye of the beholder: Neighbourhood embeddings and housing prices
entries.speaker: Stephan Heblich
entries.abstract: Urban neighborhoods differ along dozens of dimensions simultaneously, from building stock and greenery to walkability and transport access, yet these amenities are difficult to measure systematically at a spatial scale relevant for residential choice. This paper develops a framework for measuring neighborhood amenities from street-level and aerial imagery and embedding them into a quantitative spatial model. Using Google Street View panoramas and aerial images linked to more than one million housing transactions in the Paris metropolitan area, we construct visual embeddings summarizing the urban environment at a 50-meter resolution. In hedonic regressions, these embeddings explain a substantial share of housing price variation beyond standard housing attributes and neighborhood fixed effects. We decompose the embeddings into 62 interpretable urban concepts using a vision-language model and sparse coding, and document that their effects extend beyond the immediate location but decay rapidly with distance. We then embed these visual amenities into a quantitative spatial model of residential and workplace choice. The model recovers residential attractiveness at a granular spatial scale and decomposes it into observed visual amenities and unobserved location fundamentals. This structure allows us to quantify how counterfactual changes in the urban environment affect residential sorting and equilibrium housing prices. An extension allows households to allocate limited attention across amenity dimensions, determining which characteristics of the urban environment influence their location choices.

entries.seminar_title: Welfare with Discrete Choice in General Equilibrium
entries.speaker: Ariel Burstein
entries.abstract: Discrete-choice general-equilibrium models are widely used to study how people sort across places, sectors, and jobs, but they lack a canonical aggregate welfare statistic. This paper characterizes a general equilibrium counterpart to cost-benefit analysis. We measure aggregate welfare by the largest uniform reduction in factor productivity such that everyone can be at least as well off as in the status quo. This quantifies total surplus left once winners compensate losers, allowing prices, wages, and choices to adjust in general equilibrium. We characterize this measure using compensated supply and demand functions. A main result is a version of Hulten's theorem for discrete-choice economies: under perfect competition, the first-order welfare effect of a productivity shock to producer i is given by its sales relative to GDP, regardless of the distribution of preferences and technologies. Beyond first order, we provide approximations in terms of observable income and expenditure shares and uncompensated supply and demand elasticities. We compare this measure with common alternatives: real GDP ignores amenity value; average utility depends on arbitrary assumptions about how ordinal preferences are mapped into cardinal utils. In an application to the U.S. Interstate Highway System, we show that average-utility estimates and the optimal place-based policies they imply vary erratically across observationally equivalent representations of the same preferences, while our welfare measure is invariant to these arbitrary assumptions.
